As spring drew to a close, Zhongliang spent many evenings at chess in Zhou San's gatehouse, listening while he taught the skills a secret agent could not do without. Like a schoolmaster Zhou San handed them over one by one: secret writing, disguise, shadowing and shaking a tail. "You'll be better at it than your old man," he told him.
Zhongliang sighed and said, "You mean to make me die even harder than he did."
"All the more reason to learn from me with your whole mind." Zhou San said, "These skills will save your life when it counts."
Zhongliang asked, "Is this how you taught him too?"
Zhou San shook his head and said, "He taught me. He was the one who brought me into this trade."
Zhongliang held his tongue. On Zhou San's face he saw an expression past speech, those two eyes pits of black with no light in them at all, like the two hollows in a skull.

Sometimes Zhou San took him to hear an opera, to soak in the bathhouse, to drink a couple of cups in the little Japanese taverns. "In our trade," Zhou San said, "wherever you stand, you have to look like you belong there."
Zhongliang looked at him, curious, and asked, "Why do you never ask me why I'm willing to do this work with you?"
Without a second's thought Zhou San said, "For your children and your children's children."

That night, when the two of them had finished drinking, Zhou San took him to Fourth Avenue, pointed at a Japanese brothel, and asked whether he'd ever been. Zhongliang shook his head, thinking he could never in his life go to such a place. But Zhou San held him back and said, "You'll have to give it a try."
Zhongliang wrenched his hand free at once and glared at him, eyes wide.
Zhou San laughed and said, "You're a postman. You have to look like a postman."
"But I'm no whoremonger," said Zhongliang.
Zhou San's face went dark. "When you're needed to be a whoremonger," he said, "then a whoremonger is what you'll be."
Zhongliang paid him no mind and turned to go.
Zhou San caught him again, looked into his eyes a moment, then pointed at the wonton stall across the street and said, "Then go and eat a bowl of wonton."
With that he clasped his hands behind his back, for all the world an old lecher, and swayed off into the brothel, humming a tune.

Zhongliang's bowl of wonton had gone to mush by the time Zhou San came out at last, hands still behind his back, humming his tune, looking more shameless than any lecher. Zhou San sat down across from Zhongliang, ordered himself a bowl of wonton, ate half, wiped his mouth, stood, and said, "Let's go."
Walking along, Zhongliang said suddenly, "So this is your revolution?"

Zhou San made no answer. Not until they were back in the post-office gatehouse, the door barred and the curtains drawn, did he become another man. He dug a little pellet of paper out of his ear, unrolled it, warmed it over a lit match, and read the characters that came up on it twice, carefully.
Zhongliang watched him the whole time, and when Zhou San had struck another match and burned the note, asked hesitantly, "You went to make a contact?"

Zhou San still ignored him. He went to the basin, washed his hands carefully clean, and only then said coldly, "This should have been your work." Zhongliang was taken aback and said, "Then why didn't you say so plainly?"

"If it were said plainly, would it still be underground work?" Zhou San turned his head, and all at once grinned. "A brothel is a fine place. Don't hold its filth against it." He came slowly over, thought a moment, and added, "When you get to my age you'll understand. Sometimes it's only on a woman's body that you can prove to yourself you're still alive."

Zhongliang's first woman was called Xiufen. Zhou San brought her to Zhongliang's home and said she was a country cousin of his, fled from the fighting; the Japanese had wanted to build a blockhouse there, so they had burned her village and killed everyone in it, and she was the only one to get out alive. "Let her wash your clothes and cook for you," Zhou San told Zhongliang. "You need someone to look after you."
Zhongliang said, "Better she look after you."
"What a thing to say." Zhou San glanced at this woman called Xiufen and said, "I'm old enough to be someone's grandfather."
With that Zhou San left.
Xiufen stood alone in the middle of the room, not daring to look at Zhongliang, only clutching the bundle in her arms as though it hid something more precious than her life.

Zhongliang sat and watched her a long while, said not a word, then rose, pulled open the door, and went to the post-office gatehouse. He fixed his eyes on Zhou San's two dull, lightless eyes and asked, "Answer me honestly. Who is she, really?"
Zhou San, calm and unhurried, laid out the chessboard, sat down at one end, and said, "I've told you. She's a woman with a hard fate."
Zhongliang stood where he was and said, "I don't believe you."
Zhou San smiled, but the smile was gone in a flash. He looked up at Zhongliang and said, "She really is a woman with a hard fate."

It was over the chess that Zhou San told the truth of it. He had never known Xiufen's parents, only that they were dead; her man had been the political commissar of the Songjiang detachment, and before their marriage was a month old the Japanese military police had cut off his head, and it still hung in the gate-arch of the Songjiang county town. "Take it as a task I'm giving you," Zhou San said gravely. "Treat her well." Zhongliang said nothing, only played game after game with him, until Zhou San yawned several times over and pressed him to go home: "You're a man with a household now."

But Zhongliang did not go home. In spite of himself he wandered down Yuyuan Road all the way to Rue Ratard and stood across the street, looking up at the second-floor balcony of the Siming Apartments. The light in that window was out now, and only a red-turbaned Indian constable walked away far off down the street. Zhongliang gazed at that black, empty window, though he knew Su Lina had long since gone he knew not where, and that No. 203 was lived in now by an aged Jewish couple.

For two nights running Zhongliang huddled in the waiting hall of the railway station. On the third evening he came home carrying half a sauced duck from Lu Gao Jian and found the place not only swept clean but with much of the furniture shifted, so that the whole space looked broader, and brighter too.

Xiufen took the sauced duck from him without a word and set the dishes on the table one by one. Zhongliang could not help asking where she'd got the money for food. Xiufen stood to one side like a serving girl, head lowered, and said she had pawned her earrings.
Zhongliang glanced up at her ears and saw that there was, after all, something delicate in this woman's brow and eyes, and said only, "Let's eat."
The two of them ate that meal in great constraint. Through the whole of it neither said a word, and there was only the sound of bowls and chopsticks knocking together in the room.

After dark Zhongliang bent over the Eight Immortals table to practice his characters, copied out sheet after sheet, covered every old newspaper he could find in the room, and only then set down the brush, as though there were no such person as Xiufen at all; then he pulled open the door and went out.

But Zhongliang went nowhere. He sat at the road-corner not far from home, and when the peddlers on both sides had packed up their stalls he slapped the dust from his backside, stood, and looked and looked down the empty street.
Zhongliang came in without lighting the lamp, stripped off his clothes, and got under the quilt. Lying rigid on the bed, he found his breath coming short.

Xiufen lay on one side of him, rigid too, neither moving nor making a sound. When Zhongliang, uncertain, groped his way over to her, she still did not move or speak. She only reached out to help him when he did not know what to do. Afterward she pushed him gently away with the same hand, sat slowly up in the dark, and climbed down from the bed.
Xiufen washed a long while in the kitchen before she came back and lay down. Zhongliang found that her body was as cold as a corpse.
